records.name: East Java
records.current_summary: Direction mixed: in February 2025 content creator Isa Zega became the first transgender detainee held in this province's women's prison (Lapas Perempuan Kelas IIA Sukun, Malang), after her file was declared complete on suspected defamation/extortion - a documented case of an authority placing a trans woman in a facility by identity rather than legal sex, contrary to the usual national pattern. Otherwise a conservative pesantren heartland with no other sub-national signal documented. Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): scored relative to the national score (0.15) for Indonesia.

sources.title: LGBTQ rights in Indonesia - Wikipedia
sources.claim: Wikipedia's country overview supplies the national framework a visitor to East Java stands under, with no province-specific carve-out: Indonesian law provides no anti-discrimination or hate-crime protections based on sexual orientation or gender identity, and legal gender change requires sex-reassignment surgery plus a judge's approval. The 2022 penal-code amendment criminalising sex outside marriage - in force from 2 January 2026 - carries up to one year's imprisonment and effectively leaves same-sex couples with no recognised legal relationship of any kind. The page dates Indonesia's UN Human Rights Council votes against the independent expert on sexual orientation and gender identity in 2016, 2022 and 2025, records the Constitutional Court's 14 December 2017 5-4 ruling rejecting a petition to criminalise gay sex, and cites a 2025 Pew survey in which 93% of Indonesians call homosexuality 'morally unacceptable'. This corroborates the record's baseline that nothing in civil law constrains how East Java authorities handled the Isa Zega case - a trans woman was placed in a women's prison facility by identity with no anti-discrimination framework to contest it.

records.name: Kuala Lumpur
records.current_summary: Model estimate (route 3, best-knowledge delta): federal capital: scene concentrates, most anonymity. Scored relative to the national score (0.16) for Malaysia.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust profile (Malaysia, last updated 16 Dec 2025): same-sex 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' is criminalised under Penal Code 1936 Sections 377A/377B with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping (Section 377D 'gross indecency' up to two years). It records a 28 November enforcement operation in Kuala Lumpur in which over 200 people were arrested at an all-male health centre by Kuala Lumpur police, Kuala Lumpur City Hall and the Federal Territories Islamic Religious Department (Jawi), and notes enforcement with arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment since the 2018 election, with the Federal Court striking down some state Sharia criminal-code provisions as beyond state power.

Human Rights Watch/Justice for Sisters report (10 Aug 2022) documents state-sponsored discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia based on interviews with 73 LGBT people between 2018 and 2021, including people living in Kuala Lumpur; it states that each state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya have Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct, and quotes a Kuala Lumpur activist describing regression as a conservative strand of Islam gains ground. It calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity.

records.name: Negeri Sembilan
records.current_summary: This division was covered by the dedicated country dossier, which identified no deviation from the national position material enough to score separately (±0.02); it is therefore assessed at the national score.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust profile (Malaysia, last updated 16 Dec 2025) records that in November 2014 Malaysia's Court of Appeal declared section 66 of the Syariah Criminal Enactment 1992 (Negeri Sembilan), which criminalised cross-dressing, unconstitutional for breaching rights guaranteed by the Federal Constitution, and that the Federal Court has more recently struck down Sharia criminal-code provisions in Selangor and Kelantan because state legislatures lack criminal-law power. Federal criminalisation of same-sex conduct persists under Penal Code 1936 Sections 377A/377B (up to 20 years' imprisonment with whipping), with a crackdown involving arrests, prosecutions and corporal punishment since the 2018 election.

Human Rights Watch/Justice for Sisters report (10 Aug 2022) documents state-sponsored discrimination and criminalisation of LGBT people in Malaysia, based on interviews with 73 people between 2018 and 2021 including people living in Negeri Sembilan; it states that every state and the federal territories of Kuala Lumpur and Putrajaya have Sharia codes that typically criminalise same-sex conduct. It calls on lawmakers to decriminalise same-sex conduct and gender diversity and to abandon 'rehabilitation' programs and rhetoric.

records.name: Sabah
records.current_summary:
The audited sources for Sabah document Malaysia's federal and state-level framework rather than the province itself: same-sex conduct is criminalised under Section 377A with penalties up to 20 years and whipping, there is no legal gender recognition, and state-level syariah enactments penalise male cross-dressing; a 2022 human-rights report (retrieved as a fetch-time summary) documents state-backed discrimination - arrests, raids and prosecutions driven by state religious authorities - across the federation. The source files state expressly that they contain no unit-specific findings for Sabah.

Sabah is therefore assessed on the national framework alone: criminal provisions apply through the federal penal code as in the rest of Malaysia, religious-offence jurisdiction exists at state level, and no audited source supports treating this province as materially safer or harsher than the federal baseline.

sources.claim: Human Dignity Trust profile (Malaysia, last updated 16 Dec 2025) documents the federal framework this province is assessed under: same-sex 'carnal intercourse against the order of nature' is criminalised under Penal Code 1936 Sections 377A/377B with up to 20 years' imprisonment and whipping, transgender people can be targeted through the 'gross indecency' offence and state Sharia enactments prohibiting cross-dressing and 'males posing as females', with enforcement reported since the 2018 election (arrests, prosecutions, corporal punishment). The profile contains no Sabah-specific findings.

Human Rights Watch/Justice for Sisters report (10 Aug 2022) documents state-backed discrimination against LGBT people in Malaysia: arrests and criminal prosecutions at federal and state-Sharia level, a crackdown persisting since the 2018 election, and the 2021 Nur Sajat case in which a transgender woman faced a religious-affairs arrest warrant and a 122-officer search. It calls for decriminalisation of same-sex conduct and gender diversity. The report contains no Sabah-specific findings, supporting the record's assessment on the national framework alone.
